title: Power BI and Tableau: Interactive Business Dashboards
subtitle: Turn messy business data into trustworthy, interactive dashboards in Power BI or Tableau, and price and deliver them professionally.
description: An advanced, hands-on course in professional dashboard building. You will model data as a star schema, write correct measures in DAX and Tableau calculated fields, clean data with repeatable steps, design and test interactive dashboards, and then scope, price and present dashboard work for clients or employers.
outcomes: Write a dashboard brief that ties every visual to a business question and audience
Reshape flat spreadsheets into a star schema with a date table and correct relationships
Write and check measures such as margin, year-on-year growth and target variance in DAX or Tableau
Clean messy exports with repeatable Power Query or Tableau steps and reconcile totals to the source
Build an interactive, phone-friendly dashboard and document it for handover
Scope, price and propose a dashboard project, and plan 90 days toward paid BI work
audience: Women who are comfortable with spreadsheets (formulas, sorting, simple charts) and want to build professional dashboards for employers, NGOs or paying clients.
tools: A Windows laptop or desktop for Power BI Desktop (free), or a Windows or Mac computer for Tableau Public (free)
A free Tableau Public account and, optionally, a Microsoft account
Sample or public datasets (CSV or Excel)
A phone to test mobile layouts
A notebook or spreadsheet for briefs, QA logs and estimates

modules.title: Foundations: How BI Tools Think About Data
modules.overview: Before you drag a single chart onto a canvas, you need to understand what a dashboard is for, how Power BI and Tableau differ, and how both tools expect data to be shaped. This module covers the two ideas that separate professional dashboards from pretty spreadsheets: the star schema data model and correctly built measures.

lessons.title: What a business dashboard does, and how Power BI and Tableau compare
objectives: Explain the difference between a report, a chart and an interactive dashboard
Name the main parts of the Power BI and Tableau product families
Compare the free versions of each tool and their limits
Write the three business questions a dashboard must answer before building it

blocks.text: A **dashboard** is a single screen that answers a small number of important business questions at a glance, and lets the viewer explore the answer further by clicking. A spreadsheet holds the numbers. A chart shows one view of them. A dashboard combines several connected charts, headline numbers and filters so that a manager can see what is happening, where, and why, in under a minute.

blocks.name: dashboard
blocks.alt: A person looking at a screen with several charts and headline numbers
blocks.caption: A good dashboard puts the few numbers that matter on one screen and lets the viewer click to explore.

blocks.text: **Power BI** (made by Microsoft) and **Tableau** (owned by Salesforce) are the two business intelligence (BI) tools most often named in data analyst job adverts. Both connect to data, let you build a model and calculations, turn that into interactive visuals, and publish the result so other people can use it in a browser or on the phone app. Once you understand one well, about two thirds of the thinking carries straight over to the other.
The three kinds of dashboard

items: **Strategic**: for directors and boards. A few headline numbers (revenue, margin, growth against last year), usually checked monthly.
**Operational**: for supervisors running daily work. Today's orders, stock below reorder level, late deliveries. Checked daily or hourly.
**Analytical**: for analysts and managers asking "why". More filters, drill-downs and detail tables to investigate a problem.

blocks.text: Knowing which kind you are building decides almost everything else: how much detail to show, how often the data must refresh, and how many filters to offer. A director who opens a strategic dashboard on her phone between meetings will not use eight slicers. An analyst investigating why Kano sales fell will want them.
The two product families side by side

head: Question
Power BI
Tableau
rows: Free tool for learning
Power BI Desktop, free to download, runs on Windows only
Tableau Public, free, runs on Windows and Mac
Main catch with the free tool
Sharing with colleagues through the Power BI service generally needs a paid licence
Everything you save to Tableau Public is visible to anyone on the internet
Where data is cleaned
Power Query editor (its formula language is called M)
Data Source page, and Tableau Prep as a separate tool
Calculation language
DAX (Data Analysis Expressions)
Calculated fields, including LOD (level of detail) expressions
Where finished work lives
Power BI service in a browser, organised in workspaces and apps
Tableau Cloud or Tableau Server for private work, Tableau Public for public work
Phone viewing
Power BI mobile app, with a separate mobile layout you design
Tableau Mobile app, with device layouts you design

blocks.text: Neither tool is simply better. Organisations that already run Microsoft 365, Excel and Teams often choose Power BI because it fits their accounts and licences. Teams that care most about flexible, highly visual exploration often choose Tableau. Your first job when you join a company or take a client is to find out which one they already use.

blocks.title: If you only have a Mac or a phone
blocks.text: Power BI Desktop does not run on macOS. On a Mac, start with Tableau Public, which teaches the same modelling and design thinking. You can still read Power BI reports on the phone app. Building dashboards on a phone alone is not practical: plan for at least occasional access to a laptop or desktop, for example at a hub or cyber cafe.
Start from the question, not the chart

Beginners open the tool and start dragging fields onto the canvas to see what appears. Professionals start with a short written list of the questions the dashboard must answer, and who will ask them. Every visual you later add must answer one of those questions. If it answers none, it does not go on the page.

blocks.title: From raw data to a decision
items: Business question
Connect and clean data
Model and measures
Visuals and filters
Publish and share
Decision made
blocks.caption: Every stage serves the question at the start; a dashboard that leads to no decision has failed, however good it looks.

blocks.title: Worked example: turning a monthly report into three dashboard questions
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi works for a provisions distributor with four branches: Lagos, Abuja, Kano and Port Harcourt. Each month she spends about two days copying figures from four branch spreadsheets into a 20-page Word report that the managing director rarely reads past page 3.
steps: She asks the managing director what he actually checks on those first three pages. He says: total sales against target, which branch is behind, and which product categories are slipping.

She rewrites these as three dashboard questions: (1) Are we on target this month and year to date? (2) Which branch is furthest behind target, and by how much? (3) Which categories have fallen compared with the same month last year?
She notes the audience: one director, viewing monthly, mostly on his phone. That makes it a strategic dashboard with few filters.
She lists the data needed: sales lines from all four branches, monthly targets per branch, product categories, and at least 13 months of history so that "same month last year" exists.
blocks.result: Ngozi now has a one-page brief that will guide every later decision. The 20 pages shrink to three cards, two charts and one table, and the report can refresh itself instead of taking two days of copying.

blocks.text: In this course you will build skills in both tools, but you can choose one as your main tool. The lessons show the Power BI way and the Tableau way side by side wherever they differ, so whichever you choose, you will be able to talk confidently about the other in an interview.

takeaways: A dashboard answers a few important questions on one screen and lets the viewer click to explore
Decide first whether you are building a strategic, operational or analytical dashboard
Power BI Desktop is free but Windows only; Tableau Public is free but everything saved is public
Write the business questions and audience down before you build anything

activity.title: Write your first dashboard brief
steps: Choose a real or familiar business: a shop, a cooperative, a church project, an NGO programme or your employer.
Interview the person who would use the dashboard (or imagine them carefully) and write down three questions they ask every week or month.
Decide whether the dashboard is strategic, operational or analytical, and how often it would be viewed.
List the data each question needs and where that data lives today.
Decide which tool you will practise with first, based on your computer and your target employers.
activity.evidence: A one-page brief with the three questions, the audience, the dashboard type, the data list and your chosen tool.

lessons.title: Data modelling: fact tables, dimension tables and the star schema
objectives: Identify the grain of a table and separate facts from dimensions
Reshape a flat spreadsheet into a star schema
Set one-to-many relationships correctly in Power BI or Tableau
Explain why a separate date table is needed for time comparisons

blocks.text: Most business data arrives as one wide spreadsheet: every row has the date, the branch name, the branch manager, the product, its category, the customer's name, the quantity and the amount. This works for a small table but causes problems in a BI tool: the file grows huge, names get spelt differently in different rows, and calculations become slow and confusing. Both Power BI and Tableau work best when that single sheet is split into a **star schema**.
Facts and dimensions

items: A **fact table** records events you count or add up: each sale line, each payment, each attendance record. It is long (many rows) and narrow, holding mostly numbers and ID codes.
A **dimension table** describes the things involved in those events: branches, products, customers, dates. It is short (few rows) and holds descriptive text you filter and group by.
The **grain** is what one row of the fact table means, for example "one product on one invoice". Write it down. Mixing grains (some rows per invoice, some per product line) causes double counting.

blocks.name: database-tables
blocks.alt: Connected tables of data drawn as boxes and lines
blocks.caption: In a star schema, one long fact table sits in the middle and short dimension tables connect to it.

blocks.title: Layers of a sound BI model
items: Visuals and dashboards
Measures and calculations
Relationships (one-to-many)
Fact and dimension tables
Clean source data
blocks.caption: Each layer rests on the one below it, so errors in cleaning or relationships show up later as wrong numbers on the dashboard.

blocks.text: Relationships and the filter direction

Each dimension connects to the fact table with a **one-to-many relationship**: one branch appears once in the Branch table but many times in the Sales table. The column that links them is a **key**, such as BranchID. In Power BI you create these in Model view by dragging the key from the dimension onto the fact table, and you should see "1" on the dimension side and "*" on the fact side. Keep the cross-filter direction set to **Single**, so that filters flow from dimensions down to facts. Both-direction filtering is sometimes needed, but it can produce surprising totals and should be a deliberate choice, not a default.

In Tableau, you add tables on the Data Source page. In current versions, dragging a second table next to the first creates a **relationship** (a flexible link, shown as a line often called a noodle) instead of a fixed join, and Tableau works out the right level of detail for each chart. You still choose the matching key fields. Use a hard **join** only when you understand that it combines rows into one table, which can duplicate fact rows if the key is not unique.

blocks.title: The duplicate key trap
blocks.text: A dimension key must be unique. If your Product table lists product code P-104 twice (for example once as "Indomie 70g carton" and once as "Indomie carton 70g"), every sale of P-104 can be counted twice when tables are joined, and Power BI will refuse a one-to-many relationship. Remove duplicates in the dimension before you relate it.
Why you need a date table

Comparisons such as "same month last year" or "year to date" need a table holding every single date in the period, with no gaps, plus helper columns such as Year, Month number, Month name and Quarter. In Power BI you can create one with the DAX formula **Date = CALENDAR(DATE(2025,1,1), DATE(2026,12,31))**, add the helper columns, then use **Mark as date table** and relate Date[Date] to the date column in your fact table. Tableau handles dates automatically for most charts, which is one reason beginners find it quicker, but you still need complete history for year-on-year comparisons.

blocks.title: Worked example: splitting a flat sales sheet into a star
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi's distributor exports one sheet per month. Twelve months combined give 18,000 rows with 12 columns: InvoiceNo, Date, Branch, BranchCity, BranchManager, ProductCode, ProductName, Category, CustomerName, Qty, Amount and Profit.
steps: Grain: one row is one product on one invoice. She writes this at the top of her notes.
Fact table Sales keeps InvoiceNo, Date, BranchID, ProductCode, CustomerID, Qty, Amount and Profit: 18,000 rows, 8 columns.

Dimension Branch keeps BranchID, BranchName, City and Manager: 4 rows. Product keeps ProductCode, ProductName and Category: 120 rows after removing duplicates. Customer keeps CustomerID and CustomerName: 950 rows.
She builds a Date table covering 1 January 2025 to 31 December 2026: 730 rows (365 days in each year).
She creates four one-to-many relationships: Branch to Sales, Product to Sales, Customer to Sales and Date to Sales, all single direction.
Check: the branch name used to be stored 18,000 times. Now it is stored 4 times, and a manager's name change is made in one cell.
blocks.result: The model is a clear star with Sales in the middle. Filters on branch, category, customer or month now flow cleanly into every total, and the file is smaller and faster.

blocks.text: A note on spreadsheets that hold **targets**: targets are usually set per branch per month, which is a different grain from sales lines. Keep them in their own small fact table (BranchID, Month, Target) related to the Branch and Date dimensions. Never paste the monthly target onto every sales row, because summing that column would multiply the target by the number of invoices.

blocks.title: Name things for humans
blocks.text: Rename tables and columns to plain words (Sales, Branch, Product; Amount, not AMT_NGN_X). Hide key columns such as BranchID from report view so that viewers only see fields they should drag onto charts.

takeaways: Write down the grain of every fact table before you build
Facts hold events and numbers; dimensions hold descriptions you filter by
Use one-to-many relationships with single-direction filtering as the default
Dimension keys must be unique, and targets belong in their own table
Time comparisons need a complete date table

activity.title: Sketch and build a star schema
steps: Take a flat sales or activity sheet you have (or use a public practice dataset such as the Sample Superstore data widely used for Tableau practice, or the Financials sample Microsoft provides for Power BI).
Write the grain in one sentence.
On paper, draw the fact table in the middle and each dimension around it, listing their columns.
Build the tables and relationships in your chosen tool, and check every dimension key is unique.
Add a date table (Power BI) or confirm your date field is recognised as a date (Tableau).
activity.evidence: A photo of your paper sketch and a screenshot of Model view (Power BI) or the Data Source page (Tableau) showing the relationships.

lessons.title: Measures and calculations: DAX in Power BI, calculated fields in Tableau
objectives: Explain the difference between a calculated column and a measure
Write basic DAX measures with SUM, DIVIDE and CALCULATE
Write an aggregate calculated field and a FIXED LOD expression in Tableau
Avoid the average-of-ratios mistake when calculating margins and rates

blocks.text: A dashboard is only as trustworthy as its calculations. The most common errors in BI work are not chart choices but numbers that are calculated at the wrong level: a margin averaged instead of recomputed, a total that ignores a filter, a growth rate divided by zero. This lesson teaches the core calculation habits in both tools.

blocks.name: bar-chart
blocks.caption: Behind every bar is a measure; get the measure right and every chart that uses it is right.

blocks.text: Calculated columns versus measures

blocks.title: Calculated column or measure?
items: Calculated column
Measure
blocks.caption: If the answer must change when the viewer clicks a filter, it should be a measure.

blocks.text: In Power BI, create measures with **New measure** and give them clear names. Start with simple base measures, then build others on top of them. This keeps every formula short and means a correction in one place fixes every visual.

items: Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])
Total Profit = SUM(Sales[Profit])
Profit Margin = DIVIDE([Total Profit], [Total Sales])  (DIVIDE returns blank instead of an error when sales are zero)
Sales LY = CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date]))  (needs the marked date table from the last lesson)
Sales Growth % = DIVIDE([Total Sales] - [Sales LY], [Sales LY])
Lagos Sales = CALCULATE([Total Sales], Branch[City] = "Lagos")  (CALCULATE changes the filter for this one measure)

blocks.text: **CALCULATE** is the most important DAX function. It evaluates a measure after changing the filters around it. When a visual shows March 2026 for Abuja, the measure Total Sales is calculated only for those rows. Sales LY uses CALCULATE to shift the date filter back one year while keeping the Abuja filter. Learn to say in words what filter each measure applies, and you will understand most of DAX.
The same ideas in Tableau

In Tableau, fields from your data are sorted into **dimensions** (things you group by, usually shown in blue as discrete) and **measures** (numbers you aggregate, usually shown in green as continuous). Dragging a measure onto a shelf automatically applies SUM. You create new logic with **Analysis > Create Calculated Field**.

items: Profit Ratio: **SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales])**. Aggregating first, then dividing, gives the correct margin at any level.
Writing **[Profit] / [Sales]** instead computes a ratio on every row, and Tableau then sums or averages those row ratios, which is wrong for a margin.

First Purchase Date: **{FIXED [Customer ID] : MIN([Order Date])}**. This LOD expression finds each customer's first order date regardless of other filters on the view, which lets you count new versus returning customers.
Tableau has quick table calculations (right-click a measure, Quick Table Calculation) for running totals, percent of total and year-on-year growth.

blocks.title: Worked example: the average-of-ratios mistake
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi's dashboard shows profit margin by branch. Lagos sold ₦4,000,000 with ₦600,000 profit. Kano sold ₦1,000,000 with ₦300,000 profit. The director asks for the combined margin.
steps: Wrong method: average the two margins. (15% + 30%) ÷ 2 = 22.5%.
Right method: add first, then divide. Total profit 600,000 + 300,000 = ₦900,000. Total sales 4,000,000 + 1,000,000 = ₦5,000,000.
In Power BI, Profit Margin = DIVIDE([Total Profit], [Total Sales]) gives 18% in the total row automatically. In Tableau, SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) gives 18%.
blocks.result: The correct combined margin is 18%, not 22.5%. Reporting 22.5% would overstate the business's margin by 4.5 percentage points, because Kano's small sales were given the same weight as Lagos's large sales.

blocks.title: Worked example: year-on-year growth
blocks.context: For example, the Abuja branch sold ₦12,400,000 in March 2026 and ₦10,000,000 in March 2025.
steps: Sales LY for March 2026 returns ₦10,000,000.
blocks.result: The card shows +24% for Abuja in March. For a new branch with no sales last year, DIVIDE returns blank instead of an error, which is the honest answer.

blocks.text: Filter context in plain words

Every number in a visual is calculated inside a **filter context**: the set of filters coming from the row or bar it sits in, the slicers on the page, and any filters on the visual or report. When the director clicks Kano on a bar chart, every measure on the page is recalculated for Kano only. Measures are powerful precisely because they respond to this context. Calculated columns do not: they were worked out once, row by row, when the data loaded. That is why a calculated column called Margin, averaged in a visual, gives the wrong answer, while a Profit Margin measure gives the right one at every level.

A good habit is to keep all measures in one place, for example a table called Measures in Power BI or a folder in Tableau's Data pane, and to set their number format once (percentage with one decimal place, or naira with no decimals). Then every visual that uses them shows consistent numbers without extra formatting work.

blocks.title: Test every measure in a plain table first
blocks.text: Before putting a new measure on a chart, drop it into a simple table next to branch and month, and check two or three values with a calculator against the source data. This takes five minutes and catches most mistakes.

takeaways: Use measures for anything that must respond to filters; use calculated columns only to group or filter
Build simple base measures first and reuse them
Ratios must be calculated as sum divided by sum, never as an average of row ratios
CALCULATE in DAX and LOD expressions in Tableau control the level a number is calculated at
Check new measures against the source with a calculator before charting them

activity.title: Build and check five measures
steps: In your practice model, create Total Sales, Total Profit and Profit Margin (or the Tableau equivalents).
Create a same-period-last-year measure (Power BI) or a year-on-year quick table calculation (Tableau).
Put the measures in a table by branch or region and by month.
Pick two rows and recalculate them by hand or on a phone calculator from the source data.
Deliberately create the wrong average-of-ratios version and note how different the total is.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of the check table and a short note showing your hand calculations matching the tool.

quiz.q: Funmi's dashboard will be opened monthly by a board chair on her phone, mainly to see revenue against target and growth on last year. What kind of dashboard is this?
options: Strategic, with a few headline numbers
quiz.explain: A board chair checking a few headline numbers monthly needs a strategic dashboard. Many filters or hourly refresh would not suit her.

quiz.q: Ada has only a MacBook. Which free tool can she install to start building dashboards today?
quiz.explain: Tableau Public runs on Windows and Mac. Power BI Desktop runs on Windows only.

quiz.q: In a star schema for sales, which table should hold product names and categories?
options: The Sales fact table, on every row
A Product dimension table, one row per product
quiz.explain: Descriptions such as names and categories belong in a dimension table, stored once per product and related to the fact table by a key.

quiz.q: Lagos sold ₦8,000,000 with ₦800,000 profit; Kano sold ₦2,000,000 with ₦600,000 profit. What is the correct combined profit margin?
quiz.explain: Add first: profit ₦1,400,000 ÷ sales ₦10,000,000 = 14%. Averaging the branch margins (10% and 30%) would wrongly give 20%.

quiz.q: Ngozi pasted each branch's monthly target onto every sales row, and the dashboard now shows targets hundreds of times too large. What should she do?
options: Use AVERAGE instead of SUM on the target column
Delete the target and estimate it
Move targets into their own table at branch and month grain, related to Branch and Date
quiz.explain: Targets have a different grain from sales lines. Keeping them in their own fact table avoids multiplying the target by the number of invoices.

quiz.q: Which DAX measure correctly calculates sales for the same period last year?
quiz.explain: CALCULATE shifts the date filter back one year using SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR, which needs a proper date table.

modules.title: Building, Testing and Delivering Dashboards
modules.overview: This module takes you through the real build: installing the tools, cleaning messy data with Power Query or Tableau's data tools, laying out an interactive dashboard from a wireframe, and checking every number before anyone relies on it. You finish with a documented, tested dashboard.

lessons.title: Setting up and cleaning data with Power Query and Tableau's data tools
objectives: Install Power BI Desktop or Tableau Public and organise a project folder
Clean a messy export using repeatable steps instead of manual edits
Unpivot month columns into a tidy table
Explain why recorded cleaning steps beat editing the source file by hand

blocks.text: Experienced analysts often say that most of a dashboard project is spent preparing data, not designing charts. Real exports from accounting software, POS terminals, Google Forms or bank statements arrive with title rows, merged headers, mixed spellings, blank rows and numbers stored as text. This lesson sets up your tools and teaches you to clean data in a way that repeats itself automatically every month.
Setting up

items: Power BI: download **Power BI Desktop** from Microsoft (the Microsoft Store version updates itself automatically). It needs Windows. Sign-in is optional for building on your own computer.
Tableau: create a free account on the Tableau Public website and download **Tableau Public** for Windows or Mac. Remember that saving a workbook uploads it to your public profile.
Make a project folder with three subfolders: **raw** (exports exactly as received, never edited), **model** (your .pbix or Tableau workbook) and **docs** (brief, notes, screenshots).
If your data is costly to download, work from the files on your computer. Both tools work offline once installed; you only need data to publish or share.

blocks.name: data-processing
blocks.alt: A person sorting and cleaning blocks of data on a screen
blocks.caption: Cleaning steps recorded in Power Query or Tableau Prep repeat themselves on next month's file.

blocks.text: Recorded steps, not manual edits

In Power BI, choose **Get data**, pick your file, then **Transform data** to open the **Power Query editor**. Every change you make, such as removing rows or renaming a column, is recorded in the **Applied Steps** list on the right. Next month, you drop the new file into the same folder and click **Refresh**: all the steps run again. Behind the scenes Power Query writes these steps in a language called M, which you can view in the Advanced Editor but rarely need to type.

In Tableau Public, the Data Source page lets you use the **Data Interpreter** (which detects title rows and headers in Excel sheets), rename fields, change data types, split columns and pivot columns into rows. For heavier cleaning, Tableau offers a separate tool called Tableau Prep, which records steps as a flow. For practice, the Data Source page is usually enough.

blocks.title: Standard cleaning checklist
items: Remove title and blank rows
Promote headers, set data types
Trim spaces, fix spellings
Remove true duplicates
Unpivot month columns
Check row count and totals
blocks.caption: Run the same checklist on every new data source before you build a single visual.

head: Problem in the export
Power Query fix
Tableau fix
rows: Company name and date in the first 3 rows
Home > Remove Rows > Remove Top Rows, then Use First Row as Headers
Turn on Data Interpreter
Amounts stored as text with "₦" and commas
Replace Values to remove the symbol, then change type to Decimal Number
Create a calculated field with REPLACE and FLOAT, or fix in the source export settings
"Abuja", "ABUJA", "Abj" and "Abuja " in one column
Format > Trim, then Replace Values or a small mapping table
Group or alias the values, or use Tableau Prep's clean steps
One column per month (Jan, Feb, Mar...)
Select the ID columns, then Unpivot Other Columns
Select the month columns, right-click, Pivot
Same invoice line exported twice
Remove Duplicates on the columns that define a unique line
Remove in Prep, or fix before loading

blocks.title: Never clean the raw file by hand
blocks.text: If you fix spellings directly in the Excel file, next month's export will have the same problems and you will repeat the work, possibly differently. Keep raw files untouched and let recorded steps do the cleaning. This also gives you an audit trail if someone questions a number.

blocks.title: Worked example: unpivoting a target sheet
blocks.context: For example, Tunde receives a budget sheet from finance with 40 product categories down the side and 12 month columns across the top (January to December), each cell holding a sales target in naira. Visuals cannot easily filter by month when months are columns.
steps: In Power Query he removes the two title rows and promotes the next row to headers.
He selects the Category column and chooses Unpivot Other Columns. Power Query creates two new columns, Attribute (the month name) and Value (the target).
He renames them Month and Target, and changes Target to a decimal number type.
Row check: 40 categories × 12 months = 480 rows. The editor shows 480 rows, so nothing was lost.
Total check: the original sheet's grand total was ₦96,000,000. He adds a quick total in a table visual and it shows ₦96,000,000.
He adds a column that turns the month name into a proper date (the first day of each month) so the table can relate to the Date table.
blocks.result: The targets are now a tidy table of 480 rows with Category, Month and Target, ready to compare against actual sales. Next year's budget sheet will refresh through the same steps.

blocks.title: Protect personal data from the start
blocks.text: Customer names, phone numbers and account details fall under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023. If a column is not needed to answer the dashboard questions, remove it in your first cleaning step. Never upload files containing personal data to Tableau Public, and do not email raw exports through personal accounts.

Finally, record your source in your docs folder: who sent the file, the date, how it was exported, and the row count before and after cleaning. When numbers are questioned later, these notes save hours.

takeaways: Keep raw exports untouched and let recorded steps do the cleaning
Power Query's Applied Steps and Tableau's Data Source tools both repeat on refresh
Unpivot month columns into rows so that months can be filtered
Check row counts and grand totals before and after every major step
Remove personal data you do not need at the first step

activity.title: Clean one messy file end to end
steps: Find a real messy export (a POS report, a bank statement export with personal details removed, or a budget sheet with month columns).
Create the raw, model and docs folders and copy the file into raw.
Load it into Power Query or the Tableau Data Source page and apply at least four cleaning steps from the checklist.
Record the row count and grand total before and after cleaning.
Replace the raw file with a second month's file (or a copy with a few changes) and refresh to prove the steps repeat.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of the Applied Steps list (or Tableau Data Source page) and a note with the before and after row counts and totals.

lessons.title: From brief to dashboard: wireframes, layout and interactivity
objectives: Sketch a wireframe that maps every visual to a business question
Choose the right chart for comparison, trend, composition and detail
Add slicers, cross-filtering, drill-down and tooltips that help rather than confuse
Design a phone layout for viewers on mobile

blocks.text: With a brief, a clean model and tested measures, you are ready to build. Professionals do not start in the tool. They start with a **wireframe**: a rough sketch on paper or in a slide showing where each card, chart and filter will sit, and which business question each one answers. A wireframe takes ten minutes and saves hours of rearranging.

blocks.name: visual-data
blocks.alt: A person arranging charts and panels on a large screen
blocks.caption: Lay out the dashboard on paper first, so that every panel has a question to answer.

blocks.text: Reading order and layout

People scan a screen from the top left, across, then down. Put the most important headline numbers (**KPI cards**) across the top, the main trend or comparison chart in the middle, and detail tables at the bottom. Put filters in one consistent place, either along the top or down the left side. Keep two or three colours: one neutral colour for most bars, one highlight colour for what needs attention, and red or amber only for real warnings.

head: Question type
Good chart
Avoid
rows: Compare branches or categories
Sorted horizontal bar chart
3D bars, pie charts with more than 4 or 5 slices
Trend over months
Line chart with months in order
Bars when you have more than about 12 periods
Actual against target
Bar with a target line, or a bullet chart; KPI card with variance
Gauges that take space and show one number
Share of a total (few parts)
Stacked bar or a simple 100% bar
Donut charts with many tiny slices
Exact values for checking
Table or matrix with conditional formatting
Packing exact numbers onto chart labels
Where (by state or city)
Filled or bubble map, only if location matters to the decision
Maps used just for decoration

blocks.title: Which visual for which need
items: Trend: line chart
Comparison: sorted bar
Detail: table or matrix
Headline: KPI card
axes: Over time versus at one point
blocks.caption: Place each visual by asking whether the question is about time or a single moment, and whether the viewer needs an overview or exact detail.

blocks.text: Interactivity that helps

items: **Slicers and filters**: In Power BI, a slicer visual for Month or Branch filters the whole page. In Tableau, show a filter card by right-clicking a field on the Filters shelf and choosing Show Filter, then use Apply to Worksheets so it affects every sheet on the dashboard.

**Cross-filtering**: In Power BI, clicking a bar filters the other visuals on the page by default; use Format > Edit interactions to switch this off where it confuses. In Tableau, add a **filter action** (Dashboard > Actions) or click the filter icon on a sheet to use it as a filter.
**Drill-down**: put Year, Quarter and Month (or Region, State, Branch) in a hierarchy so viewers can click down a level. Tell them it exists; many viewers never discover it.
**Tooltips**: show extra context on hover or tap, such as last year's value or the target, without adding another chart.
**Reset**: give viewers a clear way back to the default view (a bookmark button in Power BI, or a Revert option in Tableau) so they do not get lost.

blocks.title: Worked example: wireframe for the distributor's director
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi uses her three questions from the brief: on target?, which branch is behind?, which categories are slipping? The director views monthly, mostly on his phone.
steps: Top row: three KPI cards. Sales this month (₦38.2 million), Target (₦40.0 million), Variance (−₦1.8 million, −4.5%). Check: 38.2 − 40.0 = −1.8, and 1.8 ÷ 40.0 = 4.5%.
Middle left: horizontal bar chart of variance to target by branch, sorted with the worst branch at the top. Answers question 2.
Middle right: line chart of monthly sales this year against last year. Supports question 1 over time.
Bottom: a small table of categories with sales, last year and growth %, with negative growth shown in amber. Answers question 3.
Filters: only one, a Month slicer at the top. Branch filtering happens by clicking a bar.
Phone version: in Power BI's Mobile layout (or a Tableau phone device layout) she stacks the three cards, then the branch bar chart, and leaves out the line chart.
blocks.result: Each visual on the page answers one of the three questions, the layout reads top to bottom from headline to detail, and the director can use it on his phone with one finger.

blocks.text: Keep a consistent page size and grid. In Power BI, the default 16:9 page suits laptops and projectors; in Tableau, set the dashboard size to a fixed size or an automatic range so it does not jump around. Align visuals to the same edges, leave equal space between them, and resist filling every gap.

blocks.title: Five-second test
blocks.text: Show your draft to someone for five seconds, then hide it and ask what the main message was. If they cannot say, simplify: remove a visual, enlarge the KPI cards, or add a clear title that states the finding, such as "Kano is ₦1.2m behind target this month".

Write titles that say what the chart shows in plain words, label axes with units (₦ millions, number of orders), and format numbers consistently: ₦38.2m on cards, full figures only in detail tables. These small choices make a dashboard look professional.

takeaways: Wireframe first and map every visual to a question from the brief
Headline cards on top, main charts in the middle, detail at the bottom
Match chart type to question type; sorted bars and lines cover most needs
Keep interactivity simple, tell viewers how to drill, and offer a reset
Design a separate phone layout when viewers use mobile

activity.title: Wireframe and build one dashboard page
steps: Using your brief from Module 1, sketch a wireframe on paper with each visual labelled with the question it answers.
Build the page in your chosen tool using your cleaned model and tested measures.
Add one filter and check that it affects every visual it should.
Create a phone layout with the three most important elements.
Run the five-second test with a friend or family member and note what they said.
activity.evidence: A photo of the wireframe, a screenshot of the finished page and of the phone layout, and a one-line note of the five-second test result.

lessons.title: Quality assurance: reconciling numbers, honest charts and documentation
objectives: Reconcile dashboard totals with the source system before release
Test filters, drill-downs and blank values systematically
Spot and fix misleading chart choices
Write a short data dictionary and handover note

blocks.text: A dashboard that shows one wrong number loses the viewer's trust in every other number on it. Quality assurance (QA) is the set of checks you run before anyone else sees the dashboard, and again after every major change. It has three parts: are the **numbers** right, does the **interaction** work, and is the **design** honest?

blocks.name: verify-data
blocks.alt: A person checking data on a screen with a tick mark
blocks.caption: Reconcile your totals with the source before anyone makes a decision from them.

blocks.text: 1. Reconcile the numbers

**Reconciliation** means comparing your dashboard's totals with an independent, trusted figure, such as the month-end total in the accounting system, the bank statement, or the figure finance reported. Pick at least three checks: the grand total, one branch, and one month. Differences must be explained, not ignored.

blocks.title: Worked example: finding a ₦450,000 difference
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi's dashboard shows total sales for June of ₦48,350,000. The finance team's ledger shows ₦47,900,000.
steps: Difference: 48,350,000 minus 47,900,000 = ₦450,000. The dashboard is too high.
She filters to each branch in turn. Lagos, Abuja and Kano match finance exactly. Port Harcourt is ₦450,000 too high.
In a table of Port Harcourt invoices for June, she sorts by invoice number and finds three invoices each appearing twice, each worth ₦150,000.
Check: 3 × 150,000 = ₦450,000, exactly the difference.
Cause: the branch exported mid-month and again at month end, and both files sat in the raw folder.
Fix: she adds a Remove Duplicates step on InvoiceNo and ProductCode in Power Query, refreshes, and the total becomes ₦47,900,000.
blocks.result: The dashboard now reconciles with finance. She records the cause and fix in her QA log, and adds a rule to the handover note: one export file per branch per month.

blocks.text: 2. Test the interaction

items: Click every slicer value, including "Select all" and a value with no data. Does every visual update, and do blanks show sensibly instead of errors?
Click a bar in each chart. Do the other visuals cross-filter as intended?
Drill down and back up every hierarchy.
Check that totals in tables equal the sum of their rows, especially for ratio measures.

Open the phone layout on an actual phone, on mobile data, and note how long it takes to load. In Power BI, View > Performance analyzer shows which visuals are slow; Tableau has a performance recording feature for the same purpose.

blocks.text: 3. Check the design is honest

blocks.title: Honest chart checks
items: Bar axes start at zero
Same scale on compared charts
Months in calendar order
Units shown on every axis
Colour means one thing
blocks.caption: Each check prevents a chart from exaggerating or hiding a difference, even by accident.

blocks.text: A bar chart whose axis starts at ₦40 million instead of zero can make a ₦2 million difference look like a doubling. Two charts side by side with different scales invite wrong comparisons. Line charts may use a non-zero axis when showing small changes over time, but label it clearly. Use colour consistently: if amber means "below target" on one chart, it must not mean "Kano" on another.
4. Document it
Write a short **data dictionary** and **handover note** in your docs folder. It turns your dashboard from something only you understand into something an organisation can rely on.

head: Item
What to write
rows: Sources
Each file or system, who provides it, how it is exported, and how often
Measures
Name, plain-English definition and formula, for example Profit Margin = total profit divided by total sales
Refresh
Manual or scheduled, when, and who presses refresh if manual
Known limits
For example, Port Harcourt data starts in March 2025, so year-on-year is blank before March 2026
Owner and version
Who maintains it, the version number and date, and a short change log

blocks.text: 5. Ask a real user to test it

Finally, sit with one real viewer, ideally the person who will use the dashboard most, and watch them use it without helping. Ask them to answer the three brief questions using the dashboard alone. Note where they hesitate, what they click that does nothing, and any word they do not understand. Common findings are filters hidden at the edge of the screen, abbreviations such as "YoY" or "PY" that need spelling out, and numbers without units. Fix these before release, then record the session in your QA log.

Schedule QA again whenever the data source changes, a new measure is added, or the client reports a surprising number. A quick monthly check that the grand total still matches the source catches problems early, before a director quotes a wrong figure in a meeting.

blocks.title: Keep a QA log
blocks.text: Use a simple sheet with columns: date, check performed, expected value, dashboard value, pass or fail, action taken. Clients and employers value this evidence, and you can show an anonymised version in your portfolio.

takeaways: Reconcile grand total, one branch and one month against a trusted source
Explain every difference; duplicates and missing rows are the usual causes
Test every filter, cross-filter, drill-down and blank case
Bar charts start at zero, compared charts share a scale, colours mean one thing
A data dictionary and handover note make the dashboard usable without you

activity.title: Run a full QA pass
steps: Choose three reconciliation checks and record the expected values from the source data.
Compare them with your dashboard and explain any difference.
Test every filter and interaction using the list in this lesson.
Run the five honest-chart checks and fix anything that fails.
Write a one-page data dictionary and handover note.
activity.evidence: Your QA log sheet with at least eight rows, and your data dictionary.

quiz.q: Next month's export has the same spelling problems as last month's. What is the most reliable approach?
options: Fix the spellings in Excel by hand each month
Record Replace Values steps in Power Query so they run on every refresh
Ask the branches to stop sending data
quiz.explain: Recorded cleaning steps repeat automatically on refresh, so the fix is consistent and auditable.

quiz.q: A budget sheet has 25 categories and 12 month columns. After unpivoting, how many rows should the target table have?
quiz.explain: Each category gets one row per month: 25 × 12 = 300 rows. Checking the row count confirms nothing was lost.

quiz.q: Which chart best answers "Which of our 6 branches is furthest behind target?"
options: A pie chart of sales by branch
A sorted horizontal bar chart of variance to target
A line chart of total sales by day
A map with bubbles sized by sales
quiz.explain: A sorted bar chart of variance shows the branch furthest behind at the top, answering the question directly.

quiz.q: Sales this month are ₦27 million against a ₦30 million target. What should the variance card show?
quiz.explain: 27 − 30 = −₦3 million, and 3 ÷ 30 = 10%. Variance to target is divided by the target.

quiz.q: The dashboard shows ₦62.6 million for May; finance reports ₦62.0 million. You find four invoices of ₦150,000 duplicated. What next?
options: Ignore it, the difference is under 1%
Add a remove-duplicates step, refresh, confirm ₦62.0 million and log the cause
quiz.explain: 4 × ₦150,000 = ₦600,000, which is exactly the gap. Fix it at the cleaning step, confirm the reconciliation and record it in the QA log.

quiz.q: A colleague's bar chart of branch sales starts its axis at ₦45 million, making Lagos look three times larger than Abuja. What is the honest fix?
options: Start the bar axis at zero
quiz.explain: Bar lengths must be compared from zero; a truncated bar axis exaggerates differences.

modules.title: Consulting, Pricing and Your Dashboard Career
modules.overview: Technical skill gets a dashboard built; consulting skill gets it used and paid for. This module covers discovery meetings, data access and privacy, sharing securely, pricing and scoping a project, and building a portfolio and 90-day plan that leads to paid work or a BI role.

lessons.title: Discovery: questions, audiences, data access and privacy
objectives: Run a structured discovery meeting with a client or manager
Assess data sources, refresh needs and access before agreeing to build
Choose a safe sharing method and explain row-level security
Recognise data privacy duties under Nigerian law

blocks.text: Most dashboard projects that fail do so before any chart is built: the analyst built what she assumed was needed, the data could not be accessed, or the finished dashboard could not be shared with the right people. A good **discovery** meeting prevents all three. Plan for 45 to 60 minutes, take notes, and send a written summary afterwards.

blocks.name: meeting
blocks.alt: Two people in a meeting discussing notes
blocks.caption: A structured discovery meeting turns vague wishes into a buildable brief.

blocks.text: The five areas to cover

head: Area
Questions to ask
Why it matters
rows: Decisions
What decisions will this dashboard help you make? What do you do today when a number looks bad?
A dashboard that changes no decision will be abandoned
Audience
Who will view it, how often, on what device? How comfortable are they with data?
Decides strategic versus analytical design and phone layout
Data sources
Where does each number live today? Who can export it? How messy is it? Can I see a sample?
Data preparation is usually the largest share of the work
Refresh
How fresh must the data be: monthly, weekly, daily? Who will refresh if it is manual?
Live or scheduled refresh adds cost, licences and setup
Access and privacy
Who may see what? Does anyone need to see only their own branch or region? Does the data include personal details?
Shapes sharing method, security setup and legal duties

blocks.text: Also ask what reports they use today and what they like or dislike about them. Building on a familiar report is easier to adopt than inventing something new. Ask to see one real example, and ask for a small sample export before you quote, so that you can judge how messy the data is.

blocks.title: A typical discovery sequence
items: Pre-meeting: request sample
Discovery meeting
Written summary sent
Client confirms brief
Quote and proposal
blocks.caption: Do not quote a price until the client has confirmed the written brief and you have seen real sample data.

blocks.text: Sharing safely

items: **Power BI service**: publish from Desktop to a workspace, then share the report or an app with named colleagues. Sharing with others generally needs a paid licence for each user, or a capacity licence held by the organisation. Check what the client already has before promising.
**Publish to web (Power BI)**: creates a public link anyone can open. Microsoft warns that it is for public data only. Never use it for client or staff data.
**Tableau Cloud or Tableau Server**: private sharing for organisations with Tableau licences.
**Tableau Public**: free, but everything saved there is public. Use only for public or invented data, for example in your portfolio.
**Static export**: a PDF or image of the dashboard sent by email or WhatsApp. Not interactive, but sometimes the simplest safe option for a small client.

blocks.text: **Row-level security (RLS)** lets one dashboard show different rows to different viewers. In Power BI you create roles in Desktop (Modeling > Manage roles) with a DAX filter, such as Branch[City] = "Kano", test them with View as, then assign people to each role in the Power BI service. Tableau achieves the same with user filters or data policies on Tableau Cloud or Server. RLS only works when the report is shared through the service; it does not protect a file you email.

blocks.title: Personal data and the law
blocks.text: The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 sets duties for anyone processing personal data, and the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) oversees it. In practice: collect only the columns you need, remove or mask names and phone numbers where totals are enough, store client files on encrypted or password-protected devices, delete copies when the project ends, and put these promises in writing. Never send login details or data exports over open WhatsApp groups.

blocks.title: Worked example: a discovery summary for an NGO programme dashboard
blocks.context: For example, Halima meets the programme manager of an NGO running savings groups for women in three states. The manager wants a dashboard for the donor and for state coordinators.
steps: Decisions: the donor checks quarterly whether membership and savings targets are being met; coordinators decide each month which groups need a field visit.
Audience: one donor officer (laptop, quarterly) and three state coordinators (phones, monthly). Halima notes this needs two pages: a strategic summary and an operational group list.
Data: monthly Google Sheets from each state, about 2,400 member rows in total, including members' names and phone numbers.
Refresh: monthly is enough. A coordinator will upload sheets to a shared folder by the 5th of each month.

Access: each coordinator should see only her own state, and the donor should see only totals, no names. Halima proposes row-level security by state and removing names and phone numbers from the model entirely, using member ID only.
Sharing: the NGO already uses Microsoft 365, so she confirms in writing which Power BI licences the four viewers will need before quoting.
blocks.result: Halima sends a one-page summary. The manager corrects one point (savings targets are per group, not per member), confirms the rest, and Halima can now scope and price the work accurately.

takeaways: Cover decisions, audience, data sources, refresh and access in every discovery meeting
See a real sample export before you quote
Publish to web and Tableau Public are for public data only
Row-level security shows each viewer only their rows when shared through the service
Collect only the personal data you need, and protect and delete it as agreed

activity.title: Run a practice discovery meeting
steps: Choose a real person with a reporting need: a business owner, a cooperative leader, a church treasurer or your manager.
Use the five-area table to plan your questions.
Hold a 30 to 45 minute conversation and take notes.
Write a one-page discovery summary covering all five areas and the recommended sharing method.
Send it to them and ask them to correct anything wrong.
activity.evidence: Your one-page discovery summary and their reply or corrections.

lessons.title: Pricing, proposals and scope control for dashboard projects
objectives: Estimate hours for each phase of a dashboard project
Turn an estimate into a fixed project price with contingency
Write a proposal that defines exactly what is included
Handle extra requests with a change request instead of free work

blocks.text: Dashboard projects are easy to underprice. The visible part, the charts, takes the least time. Data access, cleaning, reconciliation and revisions take the most, and clients cannot see that work. A clear estimate and a tightly written proposal protect both you and the client.

blocks.name: contract
blocks.alt: A person reviewing and signing a contract document
blocks.caption: A written scope says exactly which data, pages and features are included, so both sides know when the job is done.

blocks.text: Estimate by phase

Break the project into the phases you learned in Module 2 and estimate hours for each. Your first estimates will be rough; keep a record of actual hours on every project so that your estimates improve. Then decide your hourly rate from your experience level, your local market, and what similar freelancers charge on the platforms and networks you use. The naira figures below are for illustration only, not market rates.

blocks.title: Worked example: pricing a two-page sales dashboard
blocks.context: For example, Chioma is quoting the distributor's dashboard: four branch data sources, a target sheet, two report pages (director summary and branch detail), a phone layout, and one training session. She uses an illustrative rate of ₦15,000 per hour.
steps: Discovery and brief: 4 hours. Data access and cleaning (four sources plus targets): 16 hours. Model and measures: 10 hours. Building two pages and phone layout: 12 hours. QA and reconciliation: 6 hours. Training and handover: 4 hours.
Contingency of 15% for unknown data problems: 780,000 × 0.15 = ₦117,000. Subtotal: ₦897,000. She rounds to ₦900,000.
Payment plan 50 / 30 / 20: ₦450,000 deposit before starting, ₦270,000 when the first draft is approved, ₦180,000 on handover.
Optional monthly support: refresh checks and up to 6 hours of small changes, 6 × ₦15,000 = ₦90,000 per month.
blocks.result: Chioma quotes a fixed ₦900,000 for the defined scope, with a clear payment schedule and an optional ₦90,000 monthly support plan. Data cleaning is 16 of 52 hours, about 31% of the effort, which she explains to the client.

blocks.title: Handling an extra request
items: Client asks for more
Check against written scope
Estimate extra hours
Send change request
Client approves, then build
blocks.caption: Every request outside the written scope goes round this loop before you start work on it.

blocks.text: What the proposal must say

items: **Business questions** the dashboard will answer (copied from the confirmed brief).
**Data sources included**, by name, and the client's duty to provide exports or access by a set date.
**Deliverables**: number of pages, phone layout yes or no, number of measures or KPIs, training sessions, documentation.
**Revision rounds**: for example, two rounds of changes on the first draft. Further rounds are charged.
**Not included**: for example, new data sources, extra pages, licence costs, data entry, fixing the client's source systems.
**Timeline, price, payment schedule** and what happens if client data arrives late.
**Data handling**: how you will store, protect and delete their data.

blocks.title: Payment safety
blocks.text: Take a deposit before starting and receive payments into your registered business or personal account through a traceable channel such as a bank transfer or a payment link from a provider like Paystack. Be wary of overseas "clients" who send more than the agreed amount and ask for a refund of the difference; this is a common overpayment scam. Never share your banking passwords or one-time codes with anyone.
Common reasons dashboard quotes go wrong

items: The client's data is spread across many Excel files with different layouts each month, so cleaning takes far longer than estimated. Ask for three months of samples, not one.
Nobody on the client side owns the data, so exports arrive late. Name the client contact responsible in the proposal.
Licences were not discussed, and the client expected free sharing with 20 staff. Raise licence needs during discovery, and state that licence costs are paid by the client.
The "final" dashboard keeps changing because stakeholders were not consulted early. Agree who approves the draft, and limit revision rounds.

blocks.text: Put your estimate in a small spreadsheet with one row per phase, columns for estimated and actual hours, and a notes column. After each project, compare the two. If data cleaning took 24 hours instead of 16, raise that phase in your next estimate. Within a few projects your quotes will become reliable.
Value, not just hours

Hours set your minimum price. Value can justify more. If the distributor's analyst currently spends about two days each month on a manual report, the dashboard frees roughly 24 working days a year. Explain that in the proposal in plain terms. Avoid promising specific financial gains you cannot measure; describe time saved and faster decisions instead.

head: Pricing model
Best for
Watch out for
rows: Fixed project price
Well-defined dashboards after discovery
Scope creep; protect it with a written scope
Hourly or daily rate
Unclear or exploratory work, data audits
Clients may worry about open-ended cost; give estimates
Monthly retainer
Ongoing refresh, small changes, new monthly questions
Define hours included and response times

takeaways: Estimate each phase; data preparation is usually the largest
Add contingency for unknown data problems and take a deposit
List what is included and what is not, with revision rounds
Every extra request becomes a priced change request
Explain value as time saved and faster decisions, without inventing figures

activity.title: Price and propose a real project
steps: Use the discovery summary from the last lesson.
Estimate hours for each of the six phases and total them.
Choose an hourly rate, calculate the base price, add 10 to 20% contingency and round.
Write a two-page proposal using the checklist in this lesson.
Write one sample change request for a likely extra request, with hours and price.
activity.evidence: Your estimate sheet with the calculation, the two-page proposal and one sample change request.

lessons.title: Portfolio, certification and your 90-day plan
objectives: Build a portfolio of three dashboards that show different skills
Write a short case study explaining your design decisions
Describe recognised certification routes for Power BI and Tableau
Write a 90-day plan with weekly actions toward paid work or a BI role

blocks.text: Employers and clients hiring for Power BI or Tableau work want proof that you can take messy data to a trustworthy, usable dashboard. A small portfolio of well-explained projects is more convincing than a long list of tutorials completed. This lesson shows you what to build, how to present it, and how to plan the next 90 days.

blocks.name: portfolio-website
blocks.alt: A portfolio website showing several project cards
blocks.caption: Three well-explained dashboards show more skill than twenty unexplained screenshots.

blocks.text: Three projects, three skills

items: **Project 1, business sales dashboard**: a star schema with a date table, measures including margin and year-on-year growth, and a target comparison. Shows modelling and DAX or calculated fields.
**Project 2, messy data rescue**: start from a genuinely messy public dataset and document every cleaning step, row count and reconciliation. Shows Power Query or Tableau data skills and QA.

**Project 3, public interest or NGO dashboard**: use open data, for example from a national statistics office, the World Bank or an open data portal, with a clear story for a non-technical audience. Shows communication and design.

blocks.title: Never put client data in your portfolio
blocks.text: Use only public, invented or fully anonymised data with the client's written permission. Tableau Public and Power BI's Publish to web make everything visible to anyone. For client work, show screenshots with names, figures and logos removed or replaced.
Write a short case study for each

Under each dashboard, write 150 to 250 words: the business question, the audience, the data and how you cleaned it, two design decisions and why you made them (for example, "I used a sorted bar chart of variance instead of a map because the director needs to see which branch is furthest behind"), and what you checked during QA. This shows thinking, not just button clicking. Tableau Public lets you publish interactive work to a public profile; for Power BI work, share a short screen recording and screenshots, or Publish to web only for fully public data.
Certification routes

Microsoft offers the **Power BI Data Analyst Associate** certification, earned by passing **exam PL-300**. Microsoft Learn has a free learning path for it, and the exam is paid. Tableau also offers certifications, listed on Tableau's learning and certification pages; check the current names, prices and formats there before choosing, as they change. A certificate helps you pass CV screening, but your portfolio is what convinces in an interview.

blocks.title: Your 90 days
items: Days 1-30: finish two projects
Days 31-60: third project, profile
Days 61-90: apply and pitch
blocks.caption: Build proof first, then make it visible, then ask for work every week.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 90-day plan with weekly numbers
blocks.context: For example, Amaka works full time and can give 8 hours a week, about 104 hours over 13 weeks. Her goal is either a junior BI analyst role or two paid freelance dashboards.
steps: Weeks 1 to 4 (32 hours): finish Project 1 and Project 2 with case studies.
Weeks 5 to 8 (32 hours): build Project 3, set up her Tableau Public profile and a simple portfolio page, update her LinkedIn headline and CV with her three projects.

Weeks 9 to 13 (40 hours): apply to 3 suitable roles each week (15 applications in 5 weeks), and send 2 tailored pitches each week to local businesses, cooperatives or NGOs from her network (10 pitches).
Throughout: 1 hour a week on the PL-300 learning path, about 13 hours in total, with the exam booked for after day 90 if her budget allows.
Tracking: a simple sheet with date, company, role or pitch, status and follow-up date, reviewed every Sunday.
blocks.result: By day 90 Amaka has three documented dashboards, a public profile, 15 applications and 10 pitches tracked, and a clear next step. Each week has a number she can tick off, so progress is visible even before the first offer arrives.

blocks.text: Where to look for work: data analyst and BI roles in banks, fintechs, telecoms, FMCG companies, consultancies and NGOs; remote contract work through freelance platforms and your LinkedIn network; and small local businesses and associations that still report from scattered spreadsheets. Start with the people and sectors you already know. Your first paid project often comes from someone who trusts you, not from a stranger online.

In interviews, expect a practical task: you may be given a spreadsheet and an hour to build a short report, or asked to explain how you would calculate a margin or year-on-year growth. Practise explaining the difference between a measure and a calculated column, why you use a star schema, and how you reconcile totals. Bring one of your case studies and talk through a mistake you found during QA and how you fixed it; this shows the careful habits employers look for.

blocks.title: Keep learning in small steps
blocks.text: After this course, deepen one area at a time: DAX time intelligence and CALCULATE patterns, Tableau LOD expressions, or connecting to databases with SQL. Follow official documentation (Microsoft Learn and Tableau Help) as your trusted reference.

takeaways: Build three projects that each prove a different skill
Explain every project with a short case study of decisions and checks
Never publish client data; use public or anonymised data
PL-300 is Microsoft's Power BI certification exam; check Tableau's site for current options
Turn your 90 days into weekly numbers you can track

activity.title: Draft your portfolio and 90-day plan
steps: Choose datasets for your three portfolio projects and note where each comes from.
Write the case study outline for the dashboard you built in Module 2.
Decide your target: a BI role, freelance clients, or both.
Write a 13-week plan with hours and a measurable action for each week.
Create your tracking sheet with the five columns from the worked example.
activity.evidence: Your portfolio project list, one case study draft, your 13-week plan and the tracking sheet.

quiz.q: A client asks for a quote after a 10-minute phone call, before you have seen any data. What should you do first?
options: Hold a discovery meeting, get a sample export, then confirm a written brief
quiz.explain: Data preparation is usually the biggest cost. Without seeing real data and a confirmed brief, your quote is a guess.

quiz.q: Three state coordinators must each see only their own state on one shared Power BI report. What feature solves this?
options: Row-level security roles assigned in the Power BI service
Emailing each one a separate PDF from Tableau Public
quiz.explain: Row-level security filters the rows each viewer can see when the report is shared through the service.

quiz.q: Your estimate is 40 hours at ₦12,000 per hour, plus 20% contingency. What is the quote before rounding?
Midway through, a client asks for a third report page not in the proposal. What is the professional response?
options: Build it free to keep them happy
Estimate the extra hours and send a priced change request for approval
Remove a page they already approved
quiz.explain: Extra work outside the written scope goes through a change request, so the client decides with a clear price.

quiz.q: Which data is safe to publish in a Tableau Public portfolio?
options: Open data from a national statistics office or the World Bank
Your employer's staff list with names removed but salaries kept
quiz.explain: Tableau Public is public. Use only open, invented or fully anonymised data with permission.

quiz.q: Which exam leads to Microsoft's Power BI Data Analyst Associate certification?
quiz.explain: Exam PL-300 leads to the Power BI Data Analyst Associate certification.

finalQuiz.q: Before opening Power BI, what should Kemi write down first for a new dashboard?
options: The business questions, audience and how often it will be viewed
A list of every chart type available
finalQuiz.explain: Every later choice, from data to layout, follows from the questions and audience.

finalQuiz.q: Which statement about the free tools is correct?
options: Power BI Desktop runs on Mac and Windows
Tableau Public keeps your workbooks private
Power BI Desktop is Windows only, and Tableau Public saves work publicly
Both tools require a paid licence to build anything
finalQuiz.explain: Power BI Desktop runs only on Windows; anything saved to Tableau Public is public.

finalQuiz.q: A sales fact table should have one row per product per invoice. Some rows are invoice totals instead. What is the risk?
options: Mixed grain causes double counting in totals
Nothing, the tool will sort it out
finalQuiz.explain: A fact table must have one consistent grain, or invoice totals and lines will be added together.

finalQuiz.q: Branch A sold ₦6,000,000 at 10% margin; Branch B sold ₦2,000,000 at 30% margin. What is the combined margin?
finalQuiz.explain: Profit is ₦600,000 + ₦600,000 = ₦1,200,000 on sales of ₦8,000,000, which is 15%. Averaging 10% and 30% would wrongly give 20%.

finalQuiz.q: Which DAX function returns blank instead of an error when the denominator is zero?
finalQuiz.explain: DIVIDE handles division by zero safely, which is ideal for margins and growth rates.

finalQuiz.q: In Tableau, which calculated field gives each customer's first order date regardless of other filters on the view?
finalQuiz.explain: A FIXED LOD expression calculates at the customer level, ignoring the view's level of detail.

finalQuiz.q: A budget sheet has one column per month. What should you do in Power Query?
options: Unpivot the month columns into Month and Value rows
finalQuiz.explain: Unpivoting creates a tidy table where months can be filtered and related to the date table.

finalQuiz.q: Sales are ₦44 million against a ₦40 million target. What should the variance card show?
The dashboard total is ₦300,000 higher than the bank statement for the month. Which step comes first?
options: Filter by branch and month to locate the difference, then look for duplicates
finalQuiz.explain: Narrowing down by branch and period finds the source of the gap, often duplicate rows from repeated exports.

finalQuiz.q: An NGO's donor should see only totals, never member names. What is the best approach?
options: Hide the name column in the chart
Remove names and phone numbers from the model and use member IDs
finalQuiz.explain: Collecting only the data needed protects members and meets data protection duties; hidden columns can still be exposed.

finalQuiz.q: A project estimate is 50 hours at ₦10,000 per hour with 10% contingency, paid 50/30/20. What is the deposit?
Which portfolio approach is strongest for a BI job application?
options: A client's real dashboard with their data
Three dashboards on different skills, each with a short case study of decisions and QA checks
A list of software names on a CV
finalQuiz.explain: A few documented projects show modelling, cleaning, design and thinking, without exposing client data.

capstone.title: Interactive Dashboard Portfolio Project
capstone.brief: Produce a complete, tested, interactive dashboard in Power BI or Tableau from real (with permission) or public data, together with a design case study, a QA log and data dictionary, and a pricing proposal with a 90-day plan for pursuing dashboard work.
steps: Write and confirm a one-page brief with three business questions, the audience and the dashboard type.
Clean the data with recorded steps and build a star schema with a date table and single-direction relationships.
Create and hand-check at least five measures, including a ratio and a time comparison.
Wireframe, then build at least one dashboard page with KPI cards, two purposeful charts, one filter and a phone layout.
Run a full QA pass with three reconciliation checks and the honest-chart checklist, and write the data dictionary.
Write a 200-word case study explaining your design choices for the intended audience.
Prepare a priced proposal for a realistic client version of this dashboard and a 13-week plan with weekly targets.
evidence: Dashboard file or public link (public data only) plus screenshots of desktop and phone layouts
Model view or data source screenshot showing the star schema
QA log with reconciliation results and fixes
Proposal with hour estimate, price, payment schedule and exclusions
